subject: science
title: KS2 Science diagnostic
curriculum: National Curriculum in England, key stage 2 science programme of study (2013)

skills.name: Living things and the body
skills.why: Understanding plants, animals and the human body is the base for all of biology at secondary school.
skills.strong: {name} knows a lot about plants, animals and the human body and explains it clearly.
skills.developing: {name} knows the basics about living things but is less sure how bodies work and how animals adapt.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with the key facts about living things. Secondary biology builds on these, so they are worth learning now.
skills.next_step: We will use pictures, diagrams and everyday examples to make these ideas stick.

skills.name: Materials
skills.why: Knowing how materials behave and change explains everything from cooking to recycling, and it leads on to chemistry.
skills.strong: {name} understands materials well, including how they change and how mixtures can be separated.
skills.developing: {name} knows everyday materials but is less sure about changes of state and which changes can be reversed.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident about materials and how they change. This is the start of chemistry, so it is worth building now.
skills.next_step: We will use simple kitchen experiments and clear explanations to build understanding.

skills.name: Forces, light and electricity
skills.why: Forces, light and electricity explain how the world around us works, and they lead straight into secondary physics.
skills.strong: {name} explains forces, light and electricity clearly and applies them to new situations.
skills.developing: {name} knows the key facts but finds it harder to explain why things happen, such as how circuits behave.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with forces, light and electricity. These are the building blocks of physics, so they are worth securing now.
skills.next_step: We will explore each idea with simple demonstrations and plenty of 'why' questions.

skills.name: Working scientifically
skills.why: Planning fair tests and reading results is how scientists find things out, and it runs through every science topic.
skills.strong: {name} plans fair tests and reads results carefully, just like a scientist.
skills.developing: {name} knows how to measure but is less sure about fair tests and what results really show.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident planning tests and using results. This skill runs through every science topic, so it is worth real focus.
skills.next_step: We will plan and carry out small investigations together, talking through each step.

questions.ref: Y1: identify and name common animals, including mammals
questions.stem: Which of these animals is a mammal?
questions.explain: Dolphins breathe air and feed their young on milk, so they are mammals. Living in water makes 'shark' tempting, but sharks are fish; penguins are birds.

questions.ref: Y2: identify the suitability of everyday materials for particular uses
questions.stem: Which material is best for making a window?
questions.explain: Glass is transparent, so light can pass through it, and it is waterproof. The others are opaque.

questions.ref: KS1/KS2 working scientifically: use simple equipment to measure
questions.stem: Which piece of equipment would you use to measure how long a leaf is?
questions.explain: A ruler measures length. 'How long' can mean time, which is why the stopwatch is a trap.

questions.ref: Y3: recognise that light comes from a light source
questions.stem: Which of these gives out its own light?
questions.explain: The Sun is a light source. The Moon and a mirror only reflect light; this is a very common misconception about the Moon.

questions.ref: Y3: identify the functions of different parts of flowering plants
questions.stem: What is the main job of a plant's roots?
options: To attract insects to the plant
To take in water and hold the plant steady
questions.explain: Roots take in water and minerals and anchor the plant. Leaves make food; flowers attract insects and make seeds.

questions.ref: Y4: compare and group materials as solids, liquids or gases
questions.stem: Which of these is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.explain: Water is a liquid at room temperature. Sand pours, which makes some children think it is a liquid, but each grain is a solid.

questions.ref: Y4: take accurate measurements using standard units
questions.stem: Which unit would you use to measure the temperature of water?
questions.explain: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius with a thermometer.

questions.ref: Y3: compare and group materials on whether they are attracted to a magnet
questions.stem: Which of these would be attracted to a magnet?
questions.explain: Iron is a magnetic material. Many children think all metals are magnetic; aluminium and copper are not, but iron is.

questions.ref: Y6: identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system
questions.stem: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.explain: The heart pumps blood through the blood vessels. 'Lungs' is the usual wrong answer; they take in oxygen.

questions.ref: Y4: identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle
questions.stem:
Water vapour cools down and turns back into liquid water.

What is this change called?
questions.explain: Gas to liquid is condensation, as when a cold window mists up. Evaporation is the opposite change.

questions.ref: Y3/Y4: set up simple fair tests
questions.stem:
Jess wants to find out which paper towel soaks up the most water.

What must she keep the same to make it a fair test?
options: Which towel she thinks will win
The amount of water she uses
Nothing, as long as she is careful
questions.explain: The towel is what she is changing, so everything else, such as the amount of water, must stay the same.

questions.ref: Y4: recognise some common conductors and insulators
questions.stem: Which of these materials is a good conductor of electricity?
questions.explain: Copper, a metal, conducts electricity, which is why wires are made of it. Plastic and rubber are insulators used to cover the wires.

questions.ref: Y6: identify how animals are adapted to suit their environment
questions.stem:
Polar bears have thick white fur.

How does this help them survive in the Arctic?
options: It keeps them warm and hidden on the ice
It helps them see in the dark
questions.explain: Thick fur keeps heat in, and white fur is camouflage against snow and ice, which helps when hunting.

questions.ref: Y5: explain that some changes result in new materials and are not reversible
questions.stem: Which of these changes CANNOT be reversed?
questions.explain: Burning makes new materials (ash, smoke, gases), so it cannot be undone. Dissolving is reversible: the salt comes back when the water evaporates.

questions.ref: Y5/Y6: take repeat readings; record and report results
questions.stem:
Ali rolled a toy car down a ramp three times. It travelled 42 cm, 46 cm and 44 cm.

What is the mean (average) distance, in cm?
questions.explain: 42 + 46 + 44 = 132, and 132 ÷ 3 = 44 cm. An answer of 132 means the child added but did not divide.

questions.ref: Y5: identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction
questions.stem:
A ball is rolled across the grass. It slows down and stops.

Why does it slow down?
options: Magnetism pulls it into the ground
Friction between the ball and the grass slows it
questions.explain: Friction acts against the ball's movement. Gravity pulls down, not backwards.

questions.ref: Y5: know that some materials dissolve, and describe how to recover a substance from a solution
questions.stem:
Some salt has been dissolved in water.

How could you get the salt back?
questions.explain: When the water evaporates, the salt is left behind. Filtering does not work, because dissolved salt passes through the filter paper with the water.

questions.ref: Y6: recognise that living things have changed over time; offspring vary
questions.stem: Which of these statements about evolution is correct?
options: Animals change their bodies on purpose to survive
Giraffes stretched their necks, so their young had long necks
Offspring vary, and the best suited are more likely to survive
Fossils show that living things never change
questions.explain: Offspring vary, and those best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and pass on their features. The giraffe option is the classic misconception that changes during a lifetime are inherited.

questions.ref: Y6: identify evidence that supports or refutes ideas; judge how reliable results are
questions.stem:
Mo grew one plant on a sunny windowsill and one plant in a dark cupboard. After two weeks, the sunny plant had grown 8 cm and the other had grown 2 cm.

Mo says, 'This proves that all plants grow faster in light.'

Why is this conclusion not reliable?
options: He only tested one plant in each place
8 cm is too tall to be real
He should have measured in metres
questions.explain: One plant in each place is too small a test to prove something about all plants. He needs more plants and repeat tests.

questions.ref: Y6: compare and give reasons for variations in how components function, including the brightness of bulbs
questions.stem:
A circuit has one cell and one bulb. A second, identical bulb is added to the same loop of wire (in series).

What happens?
options: Both bulbs are just as bright as before
One bulb lights and the other does not
Both bulbs are dimmer than the single bulb was
questions.explain: The same cell now has to push current through two bulbs, so less current flows and both are dimmer. 'Just as bright' is the common misconception.
